story.title: Walls that work for the city
story.lead: Apartment blocks across Central Asia have big walls that face the sun all day. Today those walls soak up summer heat and make no energy. SolarSkin turns them into small power plants that also shade the building.

walls.title: The walls
walls.text: Rows of apartment blocks with large, sunny walls: plenty of space for solar modules without touching a single roof.

city.title: The pilot city
city.text: Fergana sits in a sunny valley in eastern Uzbekistan. The first SolarSkin wall is being measured here.

sustainability.title: Good for the planet, the people and the budget
sustainability.lead: SolarSkin is built to be sustainable in three ways at once. And because every claim needs proof, the dashboard measures each one.

planet.title: Planet
points: Clean electricity from sunlight, made right where it is used
Less grid power from fossil fuels, so less CO₂
Shaded walls take in less summer heat

people.title: People
points: Cooler walls can mean cooler homes in hot summers
Nothing changes inside the flats: modules mount outside
Open data that residents and the city can check

economy.title: Economy
points: Uses walls that already exist: no new land needed
A retrofit that can scale from one block to many

measure.lead: Four numbers, straight from the wall. We show nothing we didn't measure.

method.title: How we count

items.p: A low-cost sensor kit reads power, sunlight and wall temperatures every 1–5 minutes. Nothing switches or controls the building.
One wall is shaded by the modules, the other is bare. The difference between them is the cooling effect.
CO₂ uses the UNFCCC grid factor (0.55 t/MWh). Anything we estimate is labelled as an estimate.
